subtopic: TRIALS BEFORE STIPENDIARY MAGISTRATES IN MANITOBA AND SASKATCHEWAN

speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 7 to amend the criminal code (summary trials).

subtopic: TRIALS BEFORE STIPENDIARY MAGISTRATES IN MANITOBA AND SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRIALS BEFORE STIPENDIARY MAGISTRATES IN MANITOBA AND SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
This is a very simple
amendment which is proposed. In 1930 section 774 of the criminal code was amended and a special clause was inserted with regard to the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. This is the section of the code which permits the trial of certain offences before stipendiary magistrates. The same section was amended last session, but in that amendment the change made in the previous year was omitted through some oversight. The Attorney General of Manitoba and the Attorney General of Saskatchewan have directed our attention to that omission and have asked to have the section restored as it was in the amendment of 1930. That is the whole object of the bill.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: CONVEYANCE OF PROHIBITED ARTICLES BY FREIGHT, EXPRESS OR SHIP

speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 11 to amend the criminal code.

maintopic: CONVEYANCE OF PROHIBITED ARTICLES BY FREIGHT, EXPRESS OR SHIP
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CONVEYANCE OF PROHIBITED ARTICLES BY FREIGHT, EXPRESS OR SHIP
speechtext:
This amendment is drawn with the idea of preventing the conveyance of prohibited articles by freight, by express or by ship. Such articles are now prohibited from transportation under the Post Office Act, but the Post Office Department points out that they are now sent largely by express, 
and the object of the amendment is to make it an offence to send prohibited articles by express where they are not allowed to go by mail. The amendment relates chiefly to gambling devices and lottery tickets.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 8 to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The amendment to the
Juvenile Delinquents Act is also very simple. It arises from the fact that the section as it is now in the statute provides that it is an offence for anyone to contribute, promote or procure a child to become a delinquent, but it has been held by certain magistrates in certain courts that while a man may do all in his power to procure a youth to become a delinquent, if that youth does not actually become a delinquent the man is not punishable. At the request of the province of Manitoba, endorsed by six other provinces and by nearly all the childrens' aid societies in the country, it is proposed now to insert a clause providing that it shall not be a valid defence to a prosecution under this section that notwithstanding the conduct of the accused the child did not in fact become a juvenile delinquent.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Acting Minister of Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 10 to amend and consolidate the Fisheries Act.

Fisheries Act
Explain.

Mr. Duranleau moves
that said bill be now read a first time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
surely it is the correct order of procedure for an explanation to be given when it is requested.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The primary purpose
of this bill is to amend the Fisheries Act so as to make its provisions conform to the decision of the privy council, which in 1929 determined that certain portions of the Fisheries Act relating to the licensing of fish canneries, reduction plants, whale factories and so on were idtra vires. It is therefore desirable that these provisions be deleted from the existing act. In addition there are some provisions of the act that are regulatory in their character which should be deleted also. A list of the deleted sections is set out on the back of the bill under the heading "summary".
Apart from this the more important changes may be stated as these: Section 2 of the bill adds definitions of certain terms in the act so as to remove any doubt as to their meaning. Section 8 of the bill amends section 8a of the existing act so as to authorize the cancellation of fishery licences where operations thereunder are not in conformity with the law. Under the present act cancellation cannot be made until there has been a report made by a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act. As the main object in licensing those engaged in certain branches of the fisheries is to maintain proper control over them, the requirement of an inquiry by a commissioner nullifies the usefulness of the authority to cancel the licence.
There is also another important change proposed in section 20 of the bill, which amends section 31 of the existing act, having to do with the construction of fishways in power dams and other obstructions. The existing legislation merely enables the minister to require a fishway in such an obstruction after it is built if he deems such to be necessary in the public interest. In certain sections of the country dams are now being built to such a height as to make efficient fishways impracticable, as even if the fish were enabled to ascend them the young fish would be killed in coming back over the dams. The bill provides that in such instances the owners of the dams may be required to establish such fish hatchery facilities as may be necessary to maintain the fisheries.
Will the bill be sent to the committee on marine and fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
After second reading
the bill will be referred to the marine and fisheries committee.

the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

The bill introduced

subsubtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-SITUATION IN BURNABY, B.C.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask leave to move the adjournment of the house on a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, to discuss the situation that has arisen in the municipality of Burnaby in the province of British Columbia, where hundreds of men who have been employed on unemployment relief work have not received wages or payment for work so performed, on account of a dispute between the government of British Columbia and the federal government as to accounts rendered; and further, that these men are going in privation and want and their situation is of a dire and urgent nature.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-SITUATION IN BURNABY, B.C.
speechtext:
The motion which the bon. member seeks to make is regulated by standing order 31, which provides:
Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the house (when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) must be asked after the ordinary daily routine of business (standing order 15) has been concluded and before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon.
I think the time has passed, at this sitting of the house, at which the application can be received.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-SITUATION IN BURNABY, B.C.
speechtext:
At the outset, Mr. Speaker,
may I say to the Minister of Labour that I am sorry a misunderstanding has arisen re-

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Reid
garding this matter. When I spoke to him on Friday last, I can assure him that I mentioned definitely the situation in the municipality of Burnaby. Regarding the returns, I did not mention them, and I am sorry that there should have been this misunderstanding, or that the minister should not have gathered correctly what I said. It was with reference to this situation that I spoke to him on Friday when the house rose.
When the act of 1931 was first promulgated it was distinctly understood that the Dominion government would finance all undertakings, inasmuch as under the relief act of 1930 the municipalities found it difficult to do the necessary financing. It was realized at Ottawa that under the 1931 act it would be impossible for municipalities individually to raise money, owing to the condition of the bond market.
After the commencement of the works program advice was received from Victoria that they would be required to finance the unemployment work for the first thirty days. This was presumably to wait the result of the national service loan. They were advised on more than one occasion that should this loan be fully subscribed their financial worries would be over, but so far they have not received any benefit from this loan. Because of broken promises the municipality was forced to shut down all relief work for one week in December. This resulted in a good deal of local suffering and some agitation among the unemployed.
Following this a delegation from the council attended at Victoria and placed before the Minister of Finance the urgent need for prompt payment. This resulted in their receiving, on December 22, the first payment under the 1931 act made to any city or municipality in the province of British Columbia, although, mark you, the work had been proceeding continuously from shortly before October 1, 1931. On January 26 a pay was due to the workers for the preceding week but it was only after repeated telephone messages and telegrams had been sent that a small cheque was released from Victoria to help to meet the pay-roll. In making up the difference between the amount of the cheque received and the amount of the pay-roll, all the available cash and credit of the corporation was used. On February 2 another pay was due but although every possible representation was made to the federal representative, Mr. McGeough, as well as to the Minister of Finance and his deputy, up-to-date no funds have been forthcoming. The bank is adamant in refusing further advances
and it is impossible for the municipality of Burnaby to meet the pay-roll of the regular staff, which includes school teachers, members of the police department, and so forth, until the two governments pay their share of the expenditures due under the relief act.
Since the inception of this work the municipality of Burnaby has been faced with the most grievous delays on the part of the two governments. These delays have so affected the faith of the bankers that they will no longer trust any written promises but insist upon actual deposits being made. This is an example of the excuses made: Mr. McGeough and representatives of the provincial government were interviewed, at which time Mr. McGeough stated that the delay was due to the fact that no vouchers had been received at Victoria. It was pointed out that the instructions were to file the vouchers at the government office at New Westminster, but the reply was made by the provincial representative that the New Westminster office was acting under instructions from Victoria and were holding the vouchers pending further orders. Not only had the vouchers in connection with Burnaby been held there but they were holding the vouchers for all of the Fraser valley and Vancouver.
The whole council, aroused by the continued delay, attended at Victoria on December 15. They received a letter from the Minister of Finance to the supervisor of the bank stating that the agreement and moneys would 'be forthcoming not later than the end of that week. On the strength of this letter the bank advanced funds sufficient to meet a large payroll, 'but this promise was not kept. As a result, the confidence of the bankers has been so shaken that, as previously stated, they refuse to go any further unless a substantial payment is deposited with them. The bank has treated the corporation with the utmost consideration, but they realize the absurdity of this municipality attempting to finance the share of both the provincial and the Dominion governments.
The registered unemployed in this municipality number 3,332 out of a population of 25,500, or, in other words, fifty per cent of the workers are unemployed. The corporation has put 1,600 married men and single men with dependents to work. According to the agreement the government promised to take care 6f single men and transients, but, as yet, none of this class has been put to work all hough the program is now practically completed.
It is utterly impossible for the corporation to take care of the unemployment situation

Unemployment Reliej-Mr. Reid
by means of direct relief. This is quite apparent from the estimate that it would increase the taxation by two or two and one-half mills per month to take care of the corporation's share.
I would like to quote a telegram received from the Minister of Finance in Victoria. It reads as follows:
Every voucher we received for municipal work up to January 14, 1932, has been passed by us and certificates sent to Ottawa. Directly we receive cheques from Ottawa your share will be forwarded to you.
On forwarding a copy of that telegram to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) we received in reply the following telegram:
The federal government has no contact with municipalities. We act through provinces. We have already advanced the province of British Columbia in anticipation of the receipt of vouchers large sums of money and if you are not receiving payment you must look to the provincial treasurer for relief.
It is because of that I moved the adjournment of the house in order to discuss this matter. Men are suffering in th-is municipality and the 'buck is being passed by the provincial to the Dominion government and by the Dominion government back to the provincial government. We in British Columbia are in doubt as to who is really telling the truth.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-SITUATION IN BURNABY, B.C.
speechtext: The hon. member has stated the position of the federal government; will he now state the position of the provincial government?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-SITUATION IN BURNABY, B.C.
speechtext:
The claim is that all vouchers have been sent to Ottawa and immediately they receive payment, the municipality will receive its cheque. On February 3 the mem-bets of the provincial house stated that all blame lies on Ottawa, while the Dominion representative, Mr. McGeough, states the province is to blame. I submit that the municipality of Burnaby and the workers should not be made to suffer while these governments decide who is responsible. Teachers and other salaried officials have not been paid and no word has been received of further contributions from Ottawa. No cheques can be issued until additional funds are received from both the provincial and Dominion governments, but the province says: We await payment from the Dominion, and the Dominion government says: There is enough money in British Columbia to meet these payments; look to the provincial government for payment.
(Mr. Reid.]
It is because of this serious situation that I move the ladjoumment of the house. The unemployed have organized and the reeve has advised me that he will not be held responsible should any grave crisis arise.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
subsubtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-SITUATION IN BURNABY, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that this matter has been brought to the attention of the house without some notice having been given, because I believe the house is entitled to all information in connection with the operation of The Unemployment and Farm Relief Act and that information should be available to hon. members without delay. Since this matter was first brought up a few moments ago I have obtained some information which I think will in large measure clear the atmosphere so far as the government is concerned. I am not unmindful, nor do I think anyone is who is familiar with them, of the conditions prevailing in British Columbia. The position in that province is perhaps a little more difficult than in any of the other provinces. The reason is obvious. It is well known that British Columbia is blessed, or perhaps, in relation to a matter of this kind, we should say cursed, by a fine climate, with the result that it gets all the drifters and those who are engaged in seasonal occupation.
Just at this juncture I should like to make an observation-not, I may add, in any critical sense-which I think has a direct bearing on the position in which British Columbia at present finds itself. My information is that a large number of the unemployed in that province are very new arrivals in Canada, and an analysis of the figures shows that within sixteen months prior to the first of August, 1930, about 99,000 adult males were induced or invited or encouraged to come into Canada, presumably to settle on farms. A large number of them did not settle on farms. Through various influences they were urged to come here and a large number of those people either have displaced Canadian labour or are at present unemployed. A considerable number of them drifted into British Columbia.
The government's attitude towards that province is exactly the same as its attitude towards the other provinces, except that greater consideration has been given. I have no doubt the province and the municipalities out there have great difficulties to face, because the population is scattered and distances are extensive. I believe in the main the people administering the affairs of the province and the municipalities have done what they can, but their difficulties have not been

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Gordon
entirely solved. In the month of August last a representative of this government went to British Columbia and explained to the government of that province a tentative program of work, the details of which were to have been submitted by that province within two weeks. Those details did not reach Ottawa until October 28, and they were immediately reviewed. In a conference between the provincial treasurer of British Columbia and the Department of Labour, a program was adopted involving relief works amounting to approximately S6,000,000. This program was made up as follows:
Total	Dominion
expenditure proportion Municipal works.	.	$2,749,746	$1,374,873Provincial works.	.	3,250,000	1,625,000Approximately.	.	$6,000,000	$3,000,000
That is shortly the outline of the program. According to the agreement which was subsequently entered into, the Dominion government was to be supplied with full details on schedule forms to cover the different provincial and municipal projects, but even to this date we have not received from the provincial authorities the full list of the municipal projects. They may have difficulties with which I am not acquainted, but that is the fact.
According to the agreement, payments were to be made on certificates of expenditures referring to the individual schedules approved, but there was considerable delay on the part of the province in forwarding the certificates of expenditure, and as it was in need of funds to finance both provincial and municipal operations, the following advance payments were made to them by the government.
On December 1, the Dominion loaned the province $500,000 to cover the province's share of expenditures for relief purposes. On the same date, the Dominion advanced the province $500,000, being an advance payment of the Dominion's share of unemployment relief expenditures, accounts as received from the province being applied against this advance. On December 23, a further advance of $800,000 was made to the province as an advance payment against accounts to be received from the province for provincial relief expenditures. On January 20, an advance of a further $500,000 was made to the province pending the approval of accounts which, it was understood, were to be rendered to us immediately. In addition to the above, on November 25 the sum of $3,371,664.69 was advanced by way of loan to the government of British Columbia to take care of maturing obligations in New York. The above loans
and advances are secured by treasury notes of the province, so that the house will see that the Dominion government has to the full carried out the agreement with the province.
It will thus be seen that the Dominion government has advanced by way of loan $3,371,664.69 to assist the province of British Columbia in taking care of New York maturities, and has advanced the sum of $2,300,000 against works for relief purposes in that province. In addition to this, during the course of the last week a further $225,000 was advanced to the provincial authorities in order that they might carry on the work in connection with their camps. At the present time the Department of Labour has on hand for British Columbia municipal accounts amounting to approximately $225,000. These accounts are now being checked, and will immediately be credited against the advances already made to the province.
I understand from our representative in Vancouver that they have on hand certificates for provincial works amounting to about $1,000,000, which are being forwarded and which will probably be received by us to-day. When they are received and checked, they will be credited to the advances made. As further accounts are received from the province for municipal and provincial works, they will be passed for payment and credited to the advances made until the advances are wiped out. Thereafter the accounts will be paid to the province. The advance payments against accounts to be received as distinguished from loans to the province for their share of unemployment relief amount to $1,800,000, the other S500.000 being a direct loan to the province to enable it to take care of its share.
One difficulty has arisen between the federal government and the province of British Columbia, which, in the opinion of this government, is not insuperable, and that is the province has apparently been unable to forward its vouchers in accordance with the agreement promptly enough to enable it to carry out properly its financial obligations to the municipalities and to the banks. The federal government has insisted that these vouchers be forwarded promptly in accordance with the terms of the agreement entered into, but owing to the distance from Ottawa to British Columbia and to the fact that the works carried on are in areas scattered all over that great province, certain delays must necessarily occur in assembling, checking and forwarding these vouchers. Recognizing this, the federal government has made these advances in anticipation of the receipt of the

speechtext:
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) deserves the thanks of this house and of his constituents for bringing this most serious and urgent problem to the attention of the minister. I could from the city of Vancouver bring a similar problem, only one of far greater magnitude, to the attention of the minister, for they have since the 23rd of September last

received only 812,000 when they were due to have received by the 23rd of January last over 8350,000. Here we have a scheme of unemployment relief work and direct relief, a scheme which was fastened on this parliament, a scheme which was the product of the brains of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and of the present Minister of Labour, and for that scheme they and the administration must accept full and final responsibility.
What has happened in British Columbia? If I followed correctly the figures given by the Minister of Labour, he referred to the sum of 83.250,000 having been given for unemployment relief work in British Columbia. Work was commenced on the 25th day of August and ceased on the 28th day of October. Why? We from British Columbia later on in this session want a full and thorough and impartial investigation made into how every cent of this money was expended in the province of British Columbia. It did not go to the men who needed work. It went into the construction of 210 camps in the province. The very day that I left Vancouver for my duties here there were some thousands of men in the city on a straight dole, men who were supposed to get unemployment relief work from the province of British Columbia. When my hon. friend's own leader (Mr. Bennett) spoke in Calgary in the last election, he said that under no conditions would he stand for the dole as a solution of the unemployment problem throughout Canada, and now this afternoon we have the unique spectacle of the new-fledged Minister of Labour in this administration defending its policies by attacking the policies of a Tory government in British Columbia. The spectacle is unique. I repeat that we insist on knowing how much money went into the construction of these camps, and how much of the taxpayers' money went to Tory heelers and henchmen for the supplying of materials in connection with the work. We want to know all these things. We want a final accounting made to show how every cent was spent in British Columbia, because to-day, as the hon, member for New Westminster said, we have thousands of men idle and suffering privation and want because of a definite lack of cooperation between this government and the government of British Columbia. I suggest to my hon. friend the Minister of Labour that if his defence is to have any weight on the floor of this house, he should administer a severe rebuke to those in British Columbia who are so grossly maladministering the affairs of the province.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Neill

subsubtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-SITUATION IN BURNABY, B.C.
speechtext:
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that there is a very bitter feeling existing in British Columbia as regards the administration of unemployment relief. I am not here to attack the Dominion government, but rather to defend it.
I understand that this Mr. McGeough is a Dominion government appointee for the province of British Columbia. I have had no personal contact with him in any way, but those who have come in contact with him speak of him as a man of both ability and integrity, and say that he did his best in a very difficult situation. If there is any blame attaching to the Dominion government, I think it is rather for not having realized sooner the class of government ministers that they were dealing with out there, and in not realizing, as they must now realize, that they will have to take the matter more or less into their own hands before it can be settled.
In September, 1930, when the unemployment relief scheme was inaugurated, I am on record as objecting to the placing of such large administrative powers in the hands of the province. I said that the day would come when we would have complaints to make and would bring them to this house, which is the only place we can bring them, and that we would then be told that the Dominion government was powerless because it had placed the administration of the relief in the hands of the province, and therefore the Dominion government was not responsible. That is exactly what has happened. The Dominion government divested themselves of responsibility for the handling of the money they were giving out. They placed too much confidence and too much power in the hands of the province, and now they are reaping the result. I suggested then that some form of commission should be appointed to control the expenditure, and I am still of that opinion. I do not think anyone in British Columbia, no matter what his politics, will deny that the province has made a complete mess of administering relief. That is the mildest term that even the friends of the provincial government use. Inefficiency is evident at every point. The whole thing reeks with suggestions of graft and corruption. Those are strong words. We in British Columbia have got used to many things in the last few years. We have got used to the idea that if a small settler wants to eke out the scanty living he makes on his farm by a few weeks' work on the government roads, it is highly desirable, if not absolutely essential, for him to join the local Conservative organization. As I say,
we have got sort of acclimatized to those conditions, but by the blessing of God I hope that we shall never have to get accustomed to the idea, that when a man is destitute and his wife and children are hungry, if he wants to get even the trivial relief that may be afforded him, he should join some political association. I have been told that a number of registration forms were sent to a certain place accompanied with very definite intimation that no work would be forthcoming for the men unless they joined the local association.
The government started out with a scheme which if properly organized and properly carried out would have been a good one; that is a system of registration. The unfortunate thing is that it was not carried out properly and it was not done by the right people. Government agents in some places, and in others, the local police, which is a well organized and reputable body, should have had the handling of that matter. Instead, it was entrusted in some cases to political friends, and they did not make the best use of it. In some cases they stood on the sidewalk, like the man in the Bible, and urged the people to come in. "Don't you want to come in and register and get a job?" I have not the regulations before me, but I remember distinctly that they contained a notice that the registrar, whoever he might be, had no option but to register everybody who applied. Mark that! No discretion was given to the registrar to ask if the man were really destitute .-you must remember that destitution is a comparative word and that a man might be in need of work without his last cent being exhausted-I say that no latitude was given to the registrar in that regard. He had to register everyone that applied. The registration form, which I have before me is of such a character, so vaguely drawn, that a millionaire could be allowed to register. One question reads:	Have you got funds in the
bank? Well, a man might have a thousand dollars or a million dollars in the bank, and if he answered "yes" to that question and swore that his answer was correct he was eligible to get a job, and once he registered he got a ticket more or less automatically.
After the work was suddenly shut down, for reasons that I shall explain in a moment or two, a belated attempt was made to check over this list of people registered and to strike out the names of many thousands who should never 'have been put on at all. There were instances of men employed on relief work who had a 'hired man at home working for them. But when this belated attempt was

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Neill
made the "work had already been stopped, and so it was of no use because it was impossible for lack of funds to start the work going again. As my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) has said the government took it into its head to erect a large number of camps throughout the province. One might say they were equipped almost luxuriously with hot and cold water shower baths, electric lighting plants, and I am informed even radios have been provided in some cases. The tools were furnished on a scale never known before in connection with road work. Every man had enough tools to suffice for ten; every man had a wheel barrow; every man had a ten-foot saw, which was entirely unnecessary, and everything was done on a lavish scale. The material, Mr. Speaker, was all bought at the right place, you may depend. We have instances of blankets being bought at gift stores. I take it, sir, that you know what a gift store is, but if by chance you do not know may I explain it is a place where the word gift is terminated with an "e", and where one many buy trinkets for bridge parties, and things of that nature. Blankets were bought at such places for road camps.
The government of the day in British Columbia took occasion to ask this government for an enormous sium of money-something in the neighbourhood of $7,000,000 or $8,000,000. Popular gossip was-and it may have been no more than gossip, but I repeat it for what it is worth-that the intention of the government in British Columbia was, had they received this sum of money, to use it to rush an immediate election, because everybody was going to be working. There was a political straw boss on every four cross roads. An attempt was being made to go on with the Pacific Great Eastern Railway and an election was to be sprung before Christmas. To the credit of this government, (however- and I do not know whether it was through the action of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) or his then Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson)-they put their foot down and said, "No, we do not believe that you have 62,000 destitute people in British Columbia"-nor have we, Mr. Speaker. They said "we do not purpose to lend ourselves to anything of the kind; you have spent your money largely on camps; we have agreed to spend pro rata on a fifty-fifty basis for the purpose of relief work. The act suggested and all our regulations suggest that that money shall be spent on relief by giving men work to do. What have you done? You have spent yours, not in riotous living, but on

unnecessary camps; and you have hardly a good day's work to Show for the expenditure except the employment of a few carpenters who have built the camps." The government of the day said, "We will pay our share on the fifty-fifty basis, but it must be spent for some form of work."

I have no criticism to offer of the federal government; I think they were sincere last year when they voted money for unemployment relief, but I must agree with other speakers when they say that the money is being misused in British Columbia. If anything I believe this government should be congratulated upon stopping payments to the province of British Columbia, because I think it has been discovered that the British Columbia government is not capable of handling the money. Not only in Burnaby but in Prince Rupert and other places money was spent for the construction of camps while those who actually needed relief could not get work at all. Most of the men in Burnaby and nearby places received only six-teen days employment. Sixteen days in the fall of the year is not sufficient to keep a man for the winter, so I think if a man could be sent to British Columbia to take charge of affairs, as has been suggested, it would be a great help to the country at large, to the province of British Columbia and to the municipality.

It was not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to take part in this debate, but it seems to me that the reply of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) was extremely weak. Here we have a situation which has arisen because of a dispute between the federal and provincial governments as to the payment of men on relief work in the municipality of Burnaby. It has nothing whatever to do with the climate of British Columbia or with the immigration policies of past governments of this country. It is true that there may be quite a number of transients in the province of British Columbia and also in the municipality of Burnaby, but at present they are not affected by the statement made by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid).

So far as my information goes they are looked after by the provincial government in the camps that were built when the unemployment relief scheme was begun.
The main question is this: These men on unemployment relief in Burnaby are working for very low wages; they are working part time, yet, after having done their work, because of the dispute between the two governments they cannot get the pittance which is coming to them. That is the point of the whole matter, and we wish to get some assurance now that in the future they will not have to wait for their money. We do not want to hear about the climate of British Columbia; we know all about that. We do not care particularly to hear about the immigration policies of past governments; we have always protested against them. But at this time we do want to know that when these people have done their work for their low wages, they will not have to suffer further privation through having to wait for the federal and provincial governments to come to an understanding as to how and when they are to be paid.

subsubtopic: PROBLEMS OF DISTRIBUTION, PURCHASING POWER, EXCHANGE VALUES AND UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Whereas; the problem of production has been largely solved, assisted greatly by the application of scientific methods and the results of organized technical research; and
Whereas; the federal government has contributed to that end by the establishment of the National Council of Scientific Research, and by the financial assistance given to that body; and	.	.
Whereas; the problem of distribution, with the kindred questions of purchasing power and the exchange values of agricultural and other commodities, together with their relation to the growing problem of unemployment, are still unsolved, and demand immediate attention with systematized investigation and scientific study; and	.
Whereas; this can best be done at the instance of the state and by men of scientific training enabled to devote their entire time and attention to the study of this important subject;
Therefore be it resolved; that, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the establishment and maintenance of some organized body for this purpose, which body might be known as the National Council of Social and Economic Research.
He said: It will be readily understood by yourself, Mr. Speaker, and by the members of this house, that in presenting this resolution at this time and under immediate circumstances I am confronted with an unusual and rather unexpected situation. Owing to the early and unlooked-for collapse of the debate on the address, which died as it were almost in the moment of its birth, coupled with the rather striking innovation of yesterday's procedure, I have found myself with but scanty time for preparation. Yet, sir, immediate action is necessary if I am to rescue this motion from the oblivion into which it would otherwise be plunged through the procedure w'hich took place yesterday. Owing to these circumstances I shall be as brief in my address as the subject itself will permit. In this anticipated brevity 1 shall

Economic Research-Mr. Speakman
be following the precedent already set in the first part of this session, a precedent which is a bright and shining example and one which, if persisted in and followed throughout the entire session, will stand as a mark worthy of the emulation of future parliaments and future speakers.
Coming to the resolution itself, I think it will be recognized by the house as identical in purpose and in phraseology with the resolution which I presented a little less than twelve months ago. At that time I went into the question as fully and in as great detail as the forty minutes limitation would permit, and I do not propose at this time to indulge in wearisome repetition nor to traverse the same ground I covered then. Rather, I shall endeavour to bring forward and present some additional arguments in support of the resolution which has now 'been twice submitted.
In presenting the case last year I discussed as accurately and intelligently as possible the situation as it then existed. I pointed out to the best of my ability the enormous strides which had been taken during the past century in scientific attainment and engineering skill, and in our productive capabilities, based upon both. I also, to the best of my ability, paid tribute to some of the fine work done by the present National Research Council, a body composed of trained and distinguished scientists who, under the aegis of this parliament, and financed by the taxpayers of the country, have given material assistance in solving many of the technical problems with which we have been confronted, in improving our methods of production, and in enabling us to utilize more intelligently the vast and valuable natural resources which are found within the borders of the country. I stated then, and I still believe it true, that the problem of production itself has essentially been solved; that is, that while we have still much to learn as to improvement in methods we are now no longer in danger of shortage or famine. No longer is the problem that of a shortage of the necessaries of life. We have at the present time, and we are able at almost any time to produce, all the necessities and most of the luxuries which are required by the people of this country and by the civilized world. Under these circumstances, and having advanced these arguments at that time- those who are interested may read in Hansard what was said last year by various speakers on this subject-I shall confine myself to-day to the additional argument which I think may well be presented and which I hope will overcome the reluctance that at

that time was manifest on the part of the government.
If the subject at that time was of importance, and if the time was then opportune for its presentation, both of which I believe are true, then nothing so far as I can see has transpired during the twelve months that have passed to render the subject of less importance, to make the time less opportune, or to leave the subject matter of this resolution less imperative. Indeed, during those twelve months there has been a progression of events, an increasing severity in the situation itself, a growing tenseness of feeling and opinion throughout this land, which renders it even more imperative that such action as I suggest or some similar action should be taken in the interests alike of this nation and of stable government. One year ago it still seemed possible and many, if not the majority of the people, still thought that this depression was similar, save in magnitude and severity, to those which had passed from time to time over this land. Depressions have come in cyclical succession, they have waxed and waned, and each has been followed almost automatically by a period of relative prosperity. That prosperity again gave place to a succeeding depression of a somewhat similar character.
The present depression has assumed a new and more menacing character. Under former depressions the financial or economic systems suffered comparatively little damage, indeed the systems themselves and their chief devotees and beneficiaries at times were benefited by these depressions. During those periods we found a withdrawal to a large degree of the credit which had been advanced during periods of prosperity, credit which had been advanced to the people of this country at a time when money was comparatively cheap, when its purchase value was comparatively low. This credit was drawn back into the system with compounded interest during the periods of depression when money itself was dear and its purchasing value was doubled or trebled. Therefore those whom I might call the high priests of our economic system might well look with some fortitude, if not with some complacency, upon these depressions.
As I stated before, the present depression has passed this phase. No longer are the only sufferers those who have always suffered during times of depression or deflation. First there was agriculture. Agriculture always suffers first through the crash of price values, through the diminution almost to the vanish-

Economic Research-Mr. Speakman
ing point of its purchasing power and the disappearance of credit. The next to suffer always has been industrial labour which suffers through lack of employment and decreased wage levels. Suffering with them in the natural sequence are the merchants of this country who find their normal sales lessened. The weaker and smaller merchants are threatened with insolvency, while the larger and stronger concerns are threatened with vanishing profits and passed dividends. The present depression is of a changed character or rather it has assumed its true character and its sinister aspects are now generally manifested. Not only the farmer, not only the labourer, not only the small merchant is suffering to-day, but like some deadly paralysis it is penetrating further and further into the system. It is conquering-I will not say destroying-and damaging layer after layer of our industrial and economic structure. Because of the stock market crash we find that not only has the speculator lost his earnings and become reduced to penury, but that the prudent investor, the man or woman who invested in stocks and shares which in normal times were as safe as the Rock of Gibraltar, stocks and shares of sound intrinsic values like the shares of the Canadian Pacific Railway, is suffering from the effects of passed dividends. In many cases such investors have lost their sources of income and without the means of livelihood upon which they depended they have been reduced to peniury. In different parts of the country we find the curious and anomalous situation where men and women with property valued at many thousands of dollars are forced to rely upon relief because their property brings in nothing by way of income. It is a curious, a most significant and sinister situation.
As in the past these periods of depression or of deflation followed one another, many people looked upon them not only as a necessary evil, as perhaps the only imperfection in an otherwise perfect system, but even as a wholesome corrective, a species of economic purgative which cleansed the body politic. They were considered as the result of those bouts of inflation, those orgies of extravagance and over-expansion which we have heard about so frequently. To-day it has gone a little further than that. As I stated, it is creeping through the various layers of society, and everywhere throughout this country, throughout the civilized world as well, men and women are asking for leadership. They are demanding that leadership of those who for the time being are sitting in positions of authority and power. They ask
that they be led from such conditions and be restored to what may be termed normal conditions, to a better and more perfect system of society. This demand for leadership, this cry of distress is not confined at this time to a few agitators, it is not heard only amongst the ranks of agriculture or of labour, it is not heard only in this corner of the house, it is heard everywhere, in our universities, in our great cities, in the centres of industry and of economic life. Everywhere we find groups of students and intelligent and thinking citizens gathering together to study and discuss the situation which prevails. They seek a way out and they look to this parliament and this government for the leadership which they require.
As far as Canada is concerned, the responsibility lies here. To what degree has this parliament and has this government offered that leadership? Have they offered any suggestions or remedies which will bring this country to the plane which it should occupy? I remember, when this subject was brought up a little less than twelve months ago, that objections were taken to the establishment of such an organization. Those objections were two-fold. In the first place, we were told that such an organization as was suggested was entirely unnecessary. We were assured that within the ranks of the government itself or of the civil employees would be found that leadership and knowledge which was necessary and from that source would come the remedy which this country demanded. A year has passed and as far as I can see, and as far as the people of this country who are within my knowledge can see, no single step has been taken along the lines indicated. Up to the present moment two suggestions alone have emanated from this source as tending to restore prosperity and to bring to us victory over our difficulties and distress.
The first suggestion is that of relief. Unfortunately relief is a necessary thing. We all admit that it is essential and we all deplore that necessity. Not even the most optimistic can look upon relief as being in any sense a solution of the difficulty or look upon it as in any sense a factor which will do other than, as time goes on, increase the burden which rests upon us, increase the burden of public debt and make the problem more severe instead of lighter. The other suggestion-and that was brought forward the other day-was that the government itself should reduce by 10 per cent the purchasing power of its own employees. I leave it to the house
