Economic Research-Mr. Speakman
and the country whether that, though possibly a necessary step, showed any indication of leadership or of the way out.
I have sometimes been accused, when I speak as I do to-day, of being a pessimist. I am not a pessimist, nor do I preach a gospel of despair, for this reason: as I look around this country, surveying the magnitude of its achievements, the wealth of its resources, I recognize that those conditions under which we are suffering are not inevitable; they are not necessary; they are not an essential part of this country's life, but they are the result of human error, of human effort, of manmade conditions and as such they always are and always must ibe susceptible to human control. But to control them, to ride triumphant over the storm, to bring us victory and prosperity, prosperity real, lasting and enduring, we can no longer as a nation, as a civilized world, go on in the same haphazard, ruinous, competitive manner. It is useless, I 'believe, for us to sit down here talking about this and that and solace ourselves with the belief that if we only endure long enough, if we only tighten our belts a little tighter, if we only economize a little more or eat or drink or use a little less, in some mysterious, miraculous way things will right themselves.
I for one do not 'believe that. I believe in these days we require and must have a planned economy. A planned economy may be anything or nothing, but at least it indicates in the words themselves some definite purpose and some definite method by which that purpose shall be attained. We require a wise and intelligent use and distribution, not only of our great producing ability but of the products of our toil, the wealth we can produce. To do this we must first acquire a better, more complete and more accurate knowledge of the situation itself and of its causes, of our present system and of its defects, than we now possess. It is for that purpose I again urge upon the house and the government to consider and to create some such body as is indicated in the terms of this resolution.
We were told last year not only that it was unnecessary, but that if we endeavoured to build up a planned economy, if we endeavoured to set up such a body as might, assist us to that end, we were opening the doors to the dangers of bolshevism and sovietism. Surely it is nonsense to suggest that there is any relation between a council such as is indicated by this resolution and the somewhat ruthless though efficient despotism that we see in another land. There is no relativity there. We ail of us recognize that

such a system as we see in that other country is not one which would be suitable to Canada or to the temperament of its people, but we believe it is wrong to be so blinded by prejudice as to refuse to organize or to plan in order to meet and to solve our own difficulties, to utilize to the best advantage our own resources and intelligence because, forsooth, in some other country they have planned and organized along lines which we do not approve. I should be sorry if we were to show subh complete lack of intelligence as that. Can we not prove here in Canada and demonstrate to the world that an intelligent and organized cooperation of a free people can do more towards the solution of their own problems and towards the betterment of civilization as a whole than the forced and almost controlled obedience of the people of another land? The challenge is thrown out to us and surely we are men enough in this parliament and country to accept that challenge, to plan along our own lines and to prove that our way, our temperament, our freedom and our cooperation are the best. I should like to see us try that.
We are told again that our troubles are the result of world conditions over which a nation with a scattered population of
10,000,000 can have but little effect, can hold but little influence. But what is the world and what are world conditions? The world is composed of a number of single and separate nations and if each one of those nations assumes that counsel of despair, of inert inferiority, sitting there like a rabbit menaced by a snake in paralysed inertia, then world conditions themselves will swallow and destroy us. Surely it is not necessary for us to assume that attitude. Within this country we have many conditions which are within the control of our own people and we can set ourselves to the task, marshalling our forces, intelligence and resources, to meet and to conquer those conditions which are under our own control. Then and not until then, organized in that way, making the best of our own advantages, we are in a position to offer the cooperation which is essential to meet the international problems which must be approached upon an international scale. It is said, to change the metaphor, that in Holland they keep the streets in a perfect state of cleanliness by each householder keeping his own doorstep clean, and if we as a nation, and other nations would seek to remedy our own defects, to take advantage of our strength, each doing that, we would find a clean street.
The main thing, however, is this: are we to wait, to sit in inertia, to hope for something to

Economic Research-Mr. Lucas
come to pass, brought about by a power outside ourselves, or are we to adopt some means first of searching and understanding the causes of the troubles which beset us and then of using all the strength, wealth and intelligence that we possess, to meet those troubles? Which, I ask, is the better and more manly method of meeting the present situation? Difficulties are anticipated? Of course difficulties are anticipated. I assume one difficulty with which we shall be confronted if we are to consider such a national council, will be its cost at a time like this, a time of shrinking revenue, a time when the most rigid economy is necessary. I agree with the necessity of economy, wise economy, but there is such a thing as very unwise economy; there is such a thing as that economy which, if carried to excess, makes impossible in itself the rectification of the situation. I have heard, for example, of men in business who, because times were hard, cut out at the first their advertising, hoping in that way to remedy the situation. I am not in business, but I imagine that such a course would be the last one to pursue. The expenditure of a few thousand dollars, which is all that would be necessary to start in a small experimental way' a body such as this, would be money well spent if through its researches we had the least light thrown upon the present black and blind turmoil that we call civilization.
There will undoubtedly be many differences of opinion as to the details of such an organization, and it is for that reason that I refrain from dogmatizing at this time. I am simply contenting myself with enunciating a principle, the principle of research, and a method through which it may be carried on. I am not at present concerned as to the particular type of organization established. All I want to see is this, that we have a body of men of fit and proper character, and with the right kind of training, who will be placed in a position where they may devote their energies, their skill, their training and education to this greatest and most overwhelming of all our problems. It might be a body, for example, composed of representatives nominated by different industrial and other groups throughout the country. It might be one sort or another, and therefore I am not dogmatic about it at all. I am prepared to accept, and accept with gratification, any step forward which will tend to bring us out of the morass in which we find ourselves struggling to-day. Undoubtedly this suggestion, as any other suggestion, is open to criticism. The easiest thing in the world is to criticize, to point out defects, but, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the 41761-r
first duty of a critic who points out a weakness in another's suggestion is to bring forward himself a suggestion of a constructive character, which will be an improvement upon the method first suggested. I am willing to accept any suggestion of that sort.
Here we are. The year passes on and we find ourselves not having taken a single step forward. We find ourselves spending huge sums of money for relief, and we find ourselves praying for something to happen in some miraculous way that will relieve us and get us out of this inertia, not now complacent, but helpless inertia, where like Mica/wber we are simply waiting for something to turn up. It is that attitude which I challenge. Undoubtedly part of our troubles are international in character. There is the question of reparations and international obligations, all of which have a bearing on the matter. But it is unnecessary to go beyond the borders of this country to see the part which debts and indebtedness play in the problem which confronts us. I believe that the internal indebtedness of Canada is just as great a handicap and places just as great a weight upon the shoulders of our people as are the reparations which cannot be paid or the international debts which might just as well be forgotten. Within this country we have some control over our own financial affairs and our own interna! indebtedness.
I am simply suggesting lines upon which we might travel. We cannot shield ourselves behind world conditions. We cannot treat world conditions as an excuse for doing nothing ourselves within our own country. Not long ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), in addressing a great gathering of some religious body, is reported to have said, and to have said wisely and well, that only the grace of God could place Canada in the place which she should occupy. Those words were wise and true, but there is an old proverb, Mr. Speaker, that says God helps the man who helps himself, and I urge upon this government and upon parliament the organization of some such body as is suggested within this resolution as a first and essential step in selfhelp, without which we need not expect and do not deserve the help of either God or man.

subsubtopic: PROBLEMS OF DISTRIBUTION, PURCHASING POWER, EXCHANGE VALUES AND UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
As the
seconder of this resolution I wish to make a few observations. Let me first congratulate the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man) upon the very able manner in which he has presented this matter to the house. I think all who listened to his presentation of this question at the last session of parliament and again this afternoon will agree that he



Economic Research-Mr. Lucas
has presented it with such clarity and forcefulness that it is difficult to understand why the house should not at once accept the resolution unanimously.
In my opinion never was the time more opportune and never was the necessity so great for the appointment of a council such as this resolution calls for, if we are going to meet our present situation intelligently. Someone has said that times are improving. Are they? Last year our bigwigs of finance told us that prosperity was just around the corner. A year has passed, and the corner is still elusive. Is there a man to-day who knows just what the future holds in store? We have all read what Sir George Paish has said, and which was printed in the press within the last month or so. Another great economist, Sir Basil Blackett, has warned the world that action is needed to halt the crisis. I quote:
Sir Basil Blackett, British banker and industrialist, warned the world in a radio address from London that it faced a gloomier year in 1932 unless it exercised concerted control of its economic life and forestalled disastrous political troubles.
"There is a kind of optimism inborn in nearly all of us" he said in part, "which tries to console us with the comforting thought that trade depressions always right themselves somehow, and that this one will be no exception. . . . It is just this unreason that makes the prospects for 1932 seem to be so alarming, coupled with the desperately short time that is left for finding and applying the right remedies before it is too late. Both its intensity and its worldwide character make the present depression totally different from any that has gone before. Surely we have suffered enough already to make us face the facts. But are we facing the facts?
"More and more we are getting back to primitive methods of barter. We have forgotten that money was invented in order to be dealt with solely as a means of facilitating the exchange of desirable things. We have taken to using gold not as a standard of value^-but as an everyday means of making and receiving payments.
"How can a farmer expect to avoid bankruptcy if a mortgage of $5,000, which was equal in 1924 to the price of 2,500 bushels of wheat, to him represents in 1931 the price of nearly 6.000 bushels of wheat, and if things go on as they are, may represent 7,500 or more bushels in 1932.
"The first essential to recovery is a rise in wholesale prices, especially of primary products from their present disastrous low level, and then the essential next step is to stabilize the purchasing power of money.
"In the last few years the rise in the purchasing power of money and the disastrous fall in prices have redistributed the ownership of wealth as between the various classes of the community without rhyme or reason in a way that is socially most inequitable and have then gone on to cause a vast destruction of preexisting wealth, and what is even worse, a vast curtailment of the community's production of new wealth."

Our engineers and scientists, Mr. Speaker, readily overcome the most difficult problems, but our political and economical science belongs to the past, and before any real progress can be made and real and lasting prosperity can be restored many of our old ideas will have to be overhauled and scrapped or brought up to date.
Someone has said:
New times demand new measures and new men.
The world advances, and in time outgrows
The laws that in our fathers' day were best.
And, doubtless, after us, some purer scheme
Will be shaped out by wiser men than we,
Made wiser by the steady growth of truth.
To-day, Mr. Speaker, we need men with minds unafraid to travel, even though the trail be not blazed. I wish definitely to state that I am not a believer in communistic doctrines; I believe the Russian people have a problem of their own, which it is their duty to solve. Their problem however is different entirely from what we have in Canada. As the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man) pointed out we have, at least for the time being, solved the problem of production, our great task to-day is to secure the proper distribution of wealth among those who create it. That is our task, and I care not from what source I get ideas if they will help me out of the difficulty in which I find myself. The Russian people have embarked upon a wonderful experiment; as far as I am concerned I wish them God speed and trust their activities will bring a brighter and happier day to a people who have known nothing but oppression.
I am impressed with the fact that they have a problem and to meet it have adopted a plan, with a definite object in view. How much better would Canada have been to-day had we started out in the development of our great country with a definite plan before us. Speaking recently about the Royal Commission on Transportation Sir Henry Thornton is quoted in the press as saying, "The only thing wrong about the royal commission is that it did not sit forty years ago." Visualize what the difference would have been had we started out with a definite plan of railway development. To-day we are duplicating our railways and highways without any idea of the outcome. In the settlement of the three western .provinces comprising millions of acres, we had no plan. People poured in from all parts of the world and settled where they pleased. We had no plan for the development of our immense pulp and paper re-

Economic Research-Mr. MacNicol
sources with the result that that industry is demoralized, over-developed and millions of dollars have been lost.
Canada, along with the rest of the world, is in the midst of the greatest depression known to civilization. A person sitting on Mars and taking a bird's eye view of world conditions would certainly come to the conclusion that we are anything but intelligent people. My statement may seem paradoxical, but to me the one bright spot on the horizon lies in the seriousness of the situation. Great Britain, with her stubborn pride, refused to go off the gold standard until she was forced to do so. It seems to me that we will do nothing until conditions become so serious that we shall be forced to take action. We are content to cling to old methods which have served their purpose but outlived their usefulness. As the hon. member for Red Deer pointed out, our trouble to-day is entirely man made; we have created a machine of which we have nearly lost control. Control is imperative, however, or we will go under.
One great trouble to-day is the confusion of thought. Everyone admits there is something wrong, but few can agree on real causes and remedies. If our scientists can solve almost any industrial problem placed before them, surely it is not unreasonable to suppose that men with scientific training given the task of finding a solution to our social and economic ills would be able to do something to meet it.

subsubtopic: PROBLEMS OF DISTRIBUTION, PURCHASING POWER, EXCHANGE VALUES AND UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from an experience of
twenty-five years in industry I am in a position to tell the mover and seconder of the resolution that many of the great men in industry both in Canada and the United States would welcome any plan whatever to stabilize industry and to make more permanent the period of time employees might be engaged therein.
There is nothing new in the suggestion of an industrial economic council. I believe it was the great Bismarck, who in 1881, first advocated the inauguration of an advisory industrial committee in Germany. Germany did nothing with the suggestion made by Bismarck until after the war, but in 1919 when the German National Convention met at Weimar there was incorporated in their constitution provision for the setting up of an advisory council to assist in the expansion of German industry and to increase the permanency of the employment of all engaged therein. Anything which will assist in keeping our industries operating and in making 41761-71
employment more permanent has my hearty support. The German council consisted of 326 delegates, representing all of the various economic groups into which industrial peoples are divided. There was provision for equal representation by employers and employed, there being 163 representatives in each group. The council met monthly in the year 1920, met again in 1921 and again in 1922. Before the expiration of the year 1922 the German republic found the cost of the council too great, and since that time a smaller committee has been functioning in an advisory capacity. I presume the council discusses various bills pertaining to industry and economics generally, and sends its recommendation to the ministers of the German government under whose jurisdiction these various matters come.
Following the adoption by Germany of the principle of an economic council eight other European countries adopted the principle. Jugo-Slavia followed the example in 1921, and Poland adopted the principle but did not put it into effect. Spain and Portugal both adopted it, but owing to their economic and other troubles they have not operated it as yet. France adopted it in 1925 and Italy and Great Britain in 1930, while during the present year the republic to our south has had a committee meeting at Washington. That committee went further; it sent what was called referendum 58 throughout the United States, and as a result of their work the committee recommended to the government at Washington the adoption of some plan such as an economic council. Each of these countries has a different plan of operation, but only two, France and Germany, have put their plans into effect. The others have not yet shown what an economic council can do, but as I said a moment ago I am convinced that any council or advisory board that can assist industry and, through industry, assist labour, will be welcomed by the hundreds of thousands of men engaged in labour and by those controlling the capital of the plants which provide employment.
Perhaps owing to the present depression, this subject is more or less paramount to-day. Since 1790 we on this continent have gone through twenty-five periods of prosperity, and we are now in the twenty-fourth period of depression. After each of the great wars has come a period of depression. There was the Napoleonic war, the strife in Europe during the sixties and early seventies, the civil war in the United States and later the great war, and after each of those war periods the world experienced two depressions. There was the primary post-war period depression which we
100	COMMONS
Economic Research-Mr. MacNicol
had about 1920-1922, and the secondary postwar depression through which we are now passing. I have made a diligent study of each of those depressions, and I have no hesitation in saying that conditions during the present depression are being grappled with by all countries-and I may say particularly by our own country-in a better manner than was the case at any time during former depressions. It is because of that better handling of the situation that we are not now experiencing the terrible times through which the world went following the Napoleonic wars and the two depressions which came after it, or the conditions which obtained following the civil war in the United States. I want to be fair to all governments; I honestly believe they are doing the best they can under the circumstances to grapple with conditions, and that is particularly true of the government of Canada. I do not like to make narrow, partisan statements, and I would say this if any other party was in power doing the same thing. I believe in giving the present government unstinted credit for the fact that the situation is not much worse in Canada.
Why an economic council? I think as a result of the tremendous upheaval of the war, conditions have arisen that will require the best brains of every part of the country and of every group into which the people are divided. The Great war brought about a condition, particularly with regard to machinery, that did not exist in the world previous to that time. Owing to the terrific demand for man power and for material during the war, all governments encouraged their ablest men, their scientists, their technicians, their business men and their experts all along the line to produce machinery that would do away with a large part of manual labour. I do not want anyone to think I am not in favour of having the best machinery; quite the contrary. The best machinery cuts down the cost of production, and the more we cut down costs [DOT]the more we create a demand for that which the machine produces. But in my time I have seen the hours of labour shortened from twelve hours a day to eight hours a day, and if the machine is to continue to displace man power as it has in the past, then I think perhaps under present conditions-I do not advocate that it should be a permanent change-the machine should not operate too many hours.
Let me give one or two instances. In Milwaukee there was a plant manufacturing frames for motor cars. The capacity of the plant was 10,000 frames per day, and it employed 2,000 people working eight hours a

day. Owing to the war and the subsequent period of expansion, that company found it necessary to manufacture motor car frames much more quickly, so they installed a massive machine which filled the whole plant. To-day 200 men operating that machine turn out 10,000 motor car frames per day, so in that one case we have 1,800 men displaced by machinery. I could give many similar examples, but I will not go further along that line.
Then there is another situation which has developed during the last few years. Prior to 1919 there were many thousands of companies employing five men or less, and the number had been increasing all the time up to that year. But because of the demand for greater production with fewer employees many mergers took place, with the result that after 1919 the number of companies employing five men or less decreased by one-third.
So I say I believe that the best brains of the country should consider these matters. 1 do not intimate for a moment that the government are not capable of dealing with them, but in these serious times it could do no harm to call upon the best brains both inside and outside of parliament.
Let me go a step further along that line. What can an economic council plan for? A great many of the ablest men in the United States, including employers of labour, appeared before the economic committee at Washington and testified along certain lines. During an investigation I made recently I took occasion to discuss the matter with employers of labour and I am glad to say I learned that the great industrialists were all willing and anxious, as they were at Washington, to do anything they could to relieve the unemployment situation and to place the engagement of labour on a more permanent basis. One of the things suggested was a shortening of the hours of labour or the number of work days per week. Whether that is sound or not I am not prepared at the moment to say, but an advisory council could assist in the discussion of that question. Another thing: everywhere I found the employers of labour convinced that the time has come when some system should be adopted whereby men who are unemployed should be able to draw from some fund to which they have contributed and which has been built up partly as a result of their own labours. Some call this unemployment insurance. Call it what you will; I think the time has come when in periods of prosperity, when things are bounding along, industry is running full blast and wages are good, there should be some system of laying

Economic Research

Mr. Stevens
by a fund to tide men over times of depression, because such times are bound to recur. Depressions have followed one another and may continue to do so, but it is uip to the public men of to-day to consider some method of mitigating the distress of any future depression, so that conditions will not be as severe on the people, when a period of depression does come, as they are to-day.
I think an economic council might discuss some plan of re-education for men who are displaced. I have often wondered that for example a machine can be put into operation which will displace eighteen hundred men out of two thousand; and one machine operating in the city of St. Louis required seventy-four men where formerly there were seven thousand, without some provision being made to absorb the displaced men. An economic council could look into a matter of that kind and devise some system of re-education. I learned of two very good examples of re-education in the city of New York. A coal company down there decided to dismiss all teamsters and discard all wagons that had been delivering coal and instead to deliver coal by trucks. The men belonged to a teamsters' organization whose secretary must have been a very wise and able man, because apparently he had saved up enough in the treasury to purchase a truck, and with this he re-educated the teamsters in truck driving, so that when trucks began to be used not a man who could drive one was laid off. Some plan of re-education could be suggested by an economic council or whatever you choose to call such a body. I am not tied up to the name economic council or advisory council, so long as there is a body which will consider keeping men employed and industry in operation.
I am convinced that every man in this house, irrespective of party, is just as anxious as I am to support any plan that will alleviate distress, keep industry going and maintain men in employment. It is not at all a party question; it is a national question, a question in which we are all interested, and particularly the great mass of humanity in the country. I shall be happy to support any plan whatever that will achieve satisfactory results, keeping employees occupied and regulating production and consumption. I know very well that as a result of the war production has far exceeded consumption. The extent of productive machinery has brought that about and we must restore a relationship between production and consumption if we are to stabilize conditions and keep industry going. If the plan proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) and supported by the
hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) will bring about such a happy condition, it will have my hearty support.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subsubtopic: PROBLEMS OF DISTRIBUTION, PURCHASING POWER, EXCHANGE VALUES AND UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Last year the hon. member
for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) presented a resolution similar to this. It is true, as he stated a few moments ago, that at that time I questioned the practicability of the appointment of such a body and indicated to the house that within the ranks of the civil service of Canada there were men competent to study these problems and to advise upon them. I could possibly stop here and simply repeat the same thing. I do not wish, however, to be discourteous to my hon. friend or to treat lightly the very valuable proposition that he puts forward-valuable from this standpoint, that it is provocative of study and thought. I shall very briefly review the resolution and glance over the remarks so eloquently made by the hon. gentleman in support of his proposal and then, if time permits, I shall make one or two observations of my own on the general theme.
It will be noticed that the resolution postulates certain things and then proceeds to make a suggestion. In the first place, it states that the problems of production are largely solved. In a measure that is true. My hon. friend from Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNicol) has just indicated from a practical standpoint what tremendous strides science has made along the lines of production. As he observed a moment ago, there is*no news in this; it is something which almost everyone who has been studying economic questions readily recognizes. Production has made tremendous strides during recent years, particularly since the years of the Great war, when it was stimulated by the necessities which arose at that time. As far as the resolution deals with that particular phase I think it can be accepted.
Mention is made of the National Council on Scientific and Industrial Research, and in this connection I agree with the resolution. While I do not believe that Canada has made the progress which might be hoped for and which we expect ultimately to achieve in industrial and scientific research, nevertheless considerable progress has been made and the foundation has been well laid for a research body which will, I think, compare favourably with that of any other country located as Canada is.
The resolution then goes on to deal with certain unsolved problems. It states that the problem of distribution is unsolved, and mentions also the problems of purchasing power,
102	COMMONS
Economic Research-Mr. Stevens
exchange values and unemployment. These are problems imminently before the people, and they are all unsolved. The resolution then proceeds to demand a systematic investigation and scientific study of these problems by the state. The practical point in the resolution is that it calls for an organized body for this purpose.
My hon,. friend has very ably stated his case, and I compliment him, as I have on previous occasions, on the moderateness and eloquence of his language in presenting it. Cheerfully I pay tribute to his statements today. He describes the 'troubles and perplexities of different classes of people. He points out that there is undoubtedly suffering among agriculturists, small merchants and others, and he brings the description of this condition to a very simple head by calling it " the system ", I do not intend to cast reflection upon the remarks of my hon. friend, but may I say: that it is a very simple thing to come before this house or appear before any audience and describe the perplexities and embarrassments with which humanity is confronted. My hon. friend has said that we lack leadership. That is a trite saying which is heard almost daily. There is no question but that we lack leadership. We lack men, not only in this country but throughout the world, who have minds sufficiently colossal to enable them to grasp, understand and analyze these problems and then present a well worked out and complete solution therefor. I get a little restive when I hear a retailing of the problems with which we are confronted, the casting of a reflection because they are still unsolved, and nothing more. My study of history, such as it has been, and my experience in and out of parliament, has taught me one thing if it has taught me nothing else, and that is that the problems, perplexities and difficulties by which we are faced are not overcome by a mere statement of them. They are overcome by the age-old method of line upon line, precept upon precept, here a little and there a little, and in no other way. This cry for leadership might be almost characterized as the cry of the helpless. If we are going to cry for leadership, we should exhibit a little practical effort in the solving of these problems. I followed my hon. friend with great care, and while admiring his presentation I listened in vain for one practical suggestion. I ask him to reflect on that.
His final appeal both last year and this year was for the appointment of some body of men to deal with the problems to which he alludes, although he does not say how this body is
[Mr. Stevens. J
to be constituted. In that most elementary step there are perplexities. Does itfhe hon. .member want a body of men chosen from the economic staffs of our universities? Choose from the universities of Canada the most outstanding economists, gather them together and ask them to tackle this problem, and what would be the result? With all respect to the splendid intelligence of these men, many of whom I know personally; with all respect to their genuineness and the value of their researches, I venture this statement: they would labour for months, possibly for years, without bringing forward a practical solution of the problems with which we are confronted. If the objective is to be a short cut to what my hon. friend calls a planned economy; if we are expected to present to parliament or to the country some scheme which is fully worked out in all its detail, then I say to my hon. friend that failure will dog his steps from the very outset. It cannot be achieved in that way.
What does my hon. friend mean by a planned economy? That is a term to play with-I was going to say a term to trifle with. This word "plan" has been almost immortalized by the efforts of the great Soviet republic, and in saying that I cast no reflection upon that republic or its efforts. I have read a great deal in this regard, and I have been appalled at the magnitude of the task undertaken; I have been almost overwhelmed with the mass of detail which is encumbering their efforts in the working out of their great scheme. No one can study this so-called plan, really the only great economic plan before the world to-day, and fail to recognize that in a country like Canada, peopled as it is by individuals who have rooted in their very nature the most extraordinary type of individualism, the demand for free action, the right of freedom of movement from one part of the country to the other and the right to engage in any pursuit, this so-called planned economy would be very inappropriate.
My hon. friend says that in this planned economy he wants a more equitable distribution of wealth. That is an old-time, worn-out observation which I have heard for the last forty years. It is a very nice thing to have as an objective, and it is one to which we would all subscribe. But when we come to study the problem of first the cause, shall I say, using the old term, of wealth, and then the distribution of wealth, we are confronted at once with all the human elements that enter in. We are confronted with such things as human selfishness, one of the most invidi-

Economic Research-Mr. Stevens
ous and difficult elements of human nature to deal with or to overcome. My hon. friend will find this: plan out a scheme that on the surface may appear to be perfect in form, equitable in all its aspects, and yet the minute you come to put it into operation there springs up the human element with its selfish and other tendencies. Therefore it is an easy thing, I say, to present to the house a demand for leadership, for equity, for this, that and the other thing, but I notice there is a strange dearth of useful and practical suggestions of how these things can be achieved.
A word or two, if I may, regarding the general scheme. The problem is not by any means simple. My hon. friend complains that since last year nothing has been done towards the achievement of the ideals that he enunciates in the resolution. I am not so sure that my hon. friend, with all his ability and his time, has spent any more thought or energy on the study of this very problem than I have. I know I have spent many anxious hours trying, in the administration of a department over which I happen now to preside, dealing with trade and with commerce, to find out how we can influence the movement of commerce so that there may be an easier and more equitable flow of goods from one part of the world to another, and, indeed, from one part of the country to another. That is only one tiny phase of the problem, if I may say so; yet one is confronted with terrific difficulties wherever one moves. I have spent hours and days on perhaps one little item or one little detail. I could cite a dozen of them this afternoon. Let me take one problem which just occurs to me, that of the marketing of potatoes from the maritime provinces. My hon. friends from that section are aware they have certain grievances which probably they will air in the house during the next few days. I just cite that. In the department over which I preside, able officers, experienced men, are daily addressing themselves to that and to scores of other problems in the hope that they may solve them.
My hon. friend suggests-scarcely suggests, but insinuates by the very presentation of his case, that there is possible the formation of a general, broad plan which will override all those little difficulties and which will give to this country easy, smooth sailing. I confess to him frankly that I see no possibility of any such thing. At the present time-and by the way, my hon. friend rather emphasizes the existing depression and the economic conditions of to-day-there enter into this question world factors which are far beyond anything with which Canada can deal. He has already cited that. He says that will be advanced as an excuse. I do not advance it as an excuse; I advance it as a very real, definite obstacle in the way. Let us take, for instance, the question of international exchange, the present value of the moneys of the different countries of the world, something over which we have no control, something which is influenced by other factors with which I shall not deal this afternoon but which are very real. Australia, for example, has its currency at a discount of 25 per cent of Great Britain's, approximately 40 per cent of Canada's and 50 per cent of the United States. I cite just that one country as an illustration. Is it not at once apparent what an immense problem presents itself in the movement of trade among even those four countries where you have four, definite, distinct values of the currency of the country in order to make settlement for the interchange of goods? If you step outside of that realm and take, for instance, the orient, there vou have an exchange situation fluctuating hourly, which definitely makes or breaks the movement of goods over a period not of days but of hours. So one has but to cast one s vision over the world for a moment to recognize the fact that the problems confronting us are not of a character that are lying dormant, waiting for some supermind to come along and outline a scheme which will furnish a solution and the problem will immediately vanish.
I said a moment ago that these things will come, not by some plan or scheme, but rather by our tackling them step by step, day by day, and hour by hour and working them out in that way. I am not unmindful of the fact that there are certain great world economic problems that call for study and solution. For instance, the question of a stabilized world currency is undoubtedly one of the problems facing the world. I agree with my hon. friend to this extent, that unless and until something in the nature of stabilization of world currency is achieved, there will not be a condition of stabilization in the movement of commerce. In other words, you may have a market one day and lose it the next by virtue of fluctuations in exchange in countries other than the two doing the trading. But I repeat that I recognize fully that some of those problems must be faced.
Let us take, for instance, another problem, the question of shipping, of transport. We have in the last twenty years made tremendous strides in the matter of transport. As

Economic Research-Mr. Stevens
from day to day I study the problems with which one is faced, it is amazing to me to be suddenly confronted with the fact that certain ships, which in my memory I look upon as recent, are to-day absolutely obsolete, and I am told that the reason certain trade avenues are, shall I say, dropping off in their efficiency, is simply because those ships have not been replaced by modern ships. Those ships are only ten, twelve or fourteen years old. While in transport there have been tremendous strides, great developments, nevertheless the rapidity with which we are demanding the movement of goods constitutes a very real problem and that carries with it the further problem of the control, the direction of transport, whether it shall be subsidized or state owned. These are the practical problems which are confronting not this nation alone, but the nations of the world, and which are calling for solution.
Let me come now more directly to the resolution itself. My hon. friend asks, to use his own language, for some body of men and I think he said for some body of intelligent men. I have studied this question; I have approached sympathetically the kernel of his resolution, namely that we should make researches in this direction. In fact, last year, before the resolution was on the order paper at all, I had in mind that something of the character might be done. But I state to him again now that if we were to adopt this resolution and start to-morrow to organize this body, we would be confronted with a very grave difficulty and I should like to have heard from him or to hear from some other member who may yet speak upon this resolution,, some suggestion of the constitution of this body. I would not be satisfied simply with some body of intelligent men unless there was on that body representatives of practical commerce and industry; for instance, representatives of leaders of industry. I do not say that with any reflection on the workers in industry, but because the men who know the problems are the men who are actually confronted with them and are seeking solutions for them within the ambit of their own activities. Then also you would have to have leaders of commerce, leaders of shipping, and theoretical economists, men who have studied economics from a theoretical standpoint. All of these might be on such a body, and at once you recognize, when I have stated that, that we are getting an unwieldy body. I say to my hon. friend that it is very nice, very convenient sometimes, to suggest that these things should be done, but it is a very different thing to bring together a

body of men who will give practical results from their investigation.
I said last year that we had in the employment of the government, in the ranks of the civil service, some very able men. Let me briefly refer to that. In the Bureau of Statistics, for instance, we have some very able economists, men who are daily studying the movement of trade, and compiling figures and giving to the country a very excellent service in that regard. We have in the Department of Agriculture men who have been trained in agriculture and who are acquainted with the producers' standpoint and also with the marketing end. In my own department we have, in the commercial intelligence branch, men who have been trained for years in studying questions relating to the markets of the world, and so forth. In my estimation it is quite possible that we have within our own ranks to-day the intelligence and the experience necessary to give adequate study to this problem. I will go so far as to say this to my hon. friend: I will add to the studies I have already given to this question, and they are not slight, further study with a view to seeing if we cannot give effect to the idea of the resolution by utilizing those that we have in the government service, without disregarding for a moment such trained economists as may be engaged in the various universities or assisting in industry or finance and other branches.
I do, however, wish to impress upon the house that if we start out to form a body such as is called for in this resolution there i-s_ a grave danger that we will do either one of two things: Erect a body which to be representative must be so large that it will be cumbersome and useless, or have a body composed of theorists without practical experience whose utterances would have no sanction in the way of practice either by the government or by the country. That danger is there and it is very real. I do not raise these points simply to create obstacles in the way of carrying out the suggestion which has been so ably presented by my hon. friend from Red Deer, but simply because from a long and considered study of the problem I am very conscious of the difficulties which do present themselves.
It is doubtless correct to say that in these times through which we and the whole world are now passing we approach the study of economic and sociological problems in a manner different from that which we were inclined to adopt in years gone by. The rapidity of communication and transport has made of this world a very small entity. Not a day passes but one can pick up his news-

Economic Research-Mr. Mackenzie King
paper and in fifteen minutes by glancing over the headlines get a fairly good picture of the activities of the world. Not only that, but countries that one could name by the score, which ten years ago had no influence in world affairs at all, are to-day standing forth and impressing upon other countries of the world the significance of problems peculiar to themselves-countries which had no recognition whatsoever a few years ago. So we must approach these problems differently.
Then we do not look upon industrial problems to-day as we did ten or twelve years ago. We have completely outgrown the old method of conflict between employer and employee. True there are remnants of that still with us, but my hon. friends who represent labour in this house will be bound I think to acknowledge that tremendous progress has been made in that regard. Not that the whole problem has been solved, not that every man engaged in labour to-day is able to enjoy comfort and ease. Certainly that has not been achieved, but the time has passed when, in considering the problems of capital and labour, they were approached from the standpoint that one was the enemy of the other. I think that the thinkers of the world, whether they be in politics or in economics or other branches of educational thought, all recognize that it is through the spirit of cooperation that we are going to achieve the greatest successes. I do deprecate the suggestion that all we have to do is to trot out the present system and condemn it in one sweeping gesture, and suggest the replacing of it with some other system, and that that solves the problem. That is not the case and will not be the case in my estimation. There are in the system so called that we have today, many things that are good and that are worthy of being maintained and preserved, and these ought to be carefully guarded and not recklessly swept aside. On the other hand, there are no doubt grievances, inequities, faults and weaknesses which ought to be and must be corrected as rapidly as possible. But again, I submit, progress will be made in these matters more by attacking these problems day by day and step by step rather than by seeking some new and great theory that will replace the so-called theories of the present. I would suggest this to my hon. friend. If he will accept this reservation, that the suggestion contained in the resolution is presented to the government for their earnest and sympathetic study-I assure him that so far as I am concerned it will receive that, and there will also be a very genuine
effort on my part to achieve something commensurate with the ideas expressed in the resolution-if my hon. friend will accept those assurances and be agreeable to letting the resolution pass in that form, we will accept it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: PROBLEMS OF DISTRIBUTION, PURCHASING POWER, EXCHANGE VALUES AND UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I imagine that
there is no doubt about the mover of the resolution (Mr. Speakman) accepting the suggestion the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) has made, but in connection with what the minister has said I would like to repeat a remark or two I made on the last occasion when this subject was under discussion in the house.
The object of the resolution is twofold: first, affirmation of the necessity of research in social and economic questions; second, the setting up of an organized body for that purpose. Last year I pointed out to the mover of the resolution that so far as an organized body for the purpose mentioned is concerned, that body is already in existence. It would require, of course, some enlargement of point of view on -the part of the ministry to give to the existing body the additional scope which the moveT of the resolution has in mind, but we have already in existence a National Research Council. This is the abbreviated title as given in the revised statutes. The act creating the council was passed at the time of the war. Provision was made for a council for scientific and industrial research, and the act was drawn in sufficiently broad terms to enable the ministry to make use of that body for any purpose that came within not only the terms scientific and industrial research, but social and economic research as well. My recollection is that the act provides for a committee composed of four or five ministers who constitute a committee on scientific and industrial research. That committee may refer to the council anything it wishes in the way of research and in turn the council has authority to make provision for the research work referred to it.
The minister has said that the mover of the resolution has not made a practical suggestion. May I say to him that last year I made t.he practical suggestion that the government should refer to a group of expert economists or social workers the great question of the relief of unemployment, and that the body in existence to which I have referred might very well be the agency under which, for a period of at least a year, such a group might function. That suggestion was along practical lines and was one of which the ministry might
106	COMMONS
Economic Research-Mr. Mackenzie King
well have taken advantage. They have not appointed a commission to investigate unemployment relief; everything was left to a minister of the crown who has broken down through the strain and stress of his duties. We have been spending millions of dollars of public money on unemployment relief and have nothing to show for it except an increase in the public debt. On the other hand, if there had been a body of trained and interested minds working on this question the ministry might at this time have been in a position to go forward with just the sort of further action the mover of the resolution has in mind. Some practical scheme laid before this parliament relating either to unemployment insurance or to some more effective means of cooperation between the provinces and municipalities, and the Dominion government would have been a vast help in dealing with existing conditions.
I do not wish unduly to prolong the debate but I repeat that if to-morrow a bill were brought into .this house to create a national council on social and economic research such as my hon. friend has in mind, the bill would be framed on lines identical with the legislation providing for scientific and industrial research. I feel there would be no advantage in a duplication of legislation, but I do think the present measure might well be enlarged, and that the ministry might make use of the body already in existence by assigning to additional individuals the duty of research along social and economic lines.
The minister has said he would not be satisfied with certain people. May I say to him that the statute authorizes him to name whom he likes. A committee of the cabinet has the power to say who shall constitute the advisory committee of the industrial research council, and the act provides for the appointment of fifteen men. Surely the government could find in this number a sufficient number of members of a research council to serve their purposes. Did I not think the government, under the statute already in existence, could deal with social and economic questions I would support a separate act of parliament to provide as my hon. friend from Red Deer has indicated. At this time however the less there is by way of additional expenditure the better.
I am heart and soul with him in his desire to 'have social and economic questions investigated, and more attention given to them by the government of the day. Attention up to the present has been given almost exclusively to questions having to do with the increase of material wealth. Let us realize that

times are changing, and that problems affecting human life and well-being are infinitely more important than those having to do with the increase of national wealth.

At six o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, February 11, 1932
